source: Reiter (1987) A theory of diagnosis from first principles. Artificial Intelligence 32:57-95
finding: Defines a system as a pair (system description, components). The description uses an AB (abnormal) predicate. Diagnosis from first principles uses only the design and an observation, with no failure statistics. Builds explicitly on de Kleer and Genesereth. Scan was read by OCR.
numbers: Paper is 39 pages. Full adder example: 5 components (X1, X2, A1, A2, O1), input 1,0,1 gives outputs 1,0, both outputs wrong.
quote: no heuristic information about system failures is available
limits: Scanned copy, read by OCR; some symbols garbled. Theory is for a fixed, finite, a priori list of components that may fail.
agent_relevance: The agent has only the problem text and its own attempts, no failure statistics. This is the same stance: reason from the model and the observed clash, not from base rates.

source: Reiter (1987) Definition 2.4 and Principle of Parsimony
finding: A diagnosis is a minimal set of components whose being abnormal, with all others normal, makes the system description plus observation consistent. Trigger: SD + 'all normal' + OBS is inconsistent. Retracting 'all normal' for ALL components also restores consistency, so a minimality rule is needed.
numbers: Full adder has exactly 3 diagnoses: {X1}, {X2,O1}, {X2,A2}. Prop 3.1: a diagnosis exists iff SD+OBS is consistent. Prop 3.2: {} is the only diagnosis iff no conflict with observation.
quote: A diagnosis is a conjecture that some minimal set of components are faulty.
limits: Consistency only. It does not require the diagnosis to entail the observation (that is the abductive view). Minimality is subset minimality, not probability.
agent_relevance: Maps to S-states: a failing check (the clash) triggers search for the smallest set of steps or assumptions to suspend. No clash, no diagnosis: matches guardrail G1 (doubt only on a signal).

source: Reiter (1987) Definition 4.1 and Theorem 4.4 (conflict sets and hitting sets)
finding: A conflict set is a set of components that cannot all be normal given SD and OBS. Theorem 4.4: a set is a diagnosis iff it is a minimal hitting set of the collection of (minimal) conflict sets. Corollary 4.10: a single-fault diagnosis is a component in every minimal conflict set.
numbers: Definition 4.3 hitting set: intersects every set in the collection. Proof via Prop 4.2: a diagnosis is a minimal set whose complement is not a conflict.
quote: is a minimal hitting set for the collection of conflict sets
limits: Needs the conflicts. Computing them needs a sound and complete prover; undecidable for general first-order logic.
agent_relevance: Core design idea for the scaffold: each failed check yields a conflict (set of steps or assumptions that cannot all be right). Culprit candidates = minimal hitting sets of those conflicts. Plain code can do this.

source: Reiter (1987) Section 4.2-4.3 HS-tree and algorithm DIAGNOSE
finding: Builds a breadth-first tree. Each node asks the theorem prover TP for a conflict disjoint from the path so far; if none, node is marked V and the path is a diagnosis. Three pruning rules: reuse labels, close supersets of found hitting sets, remove redundant edges when a smaller conflict appears. Prover is called only when needed, never twice for the same conflict.
numbers: Example 4.7 (7 sets): 6 minimal hitting sets found with 13 accesses to F. Full adder: 5 TP calls in one run (Fig 6), 6 in another (Fig 7); only 2 or 3 of 12 possible conflicts ever computed. Davis multiplier/adder device: 5 components, 4 diagnoses {M1},{A1},{M2,M3},{A2,M2}.
quote: No two calls by DIAGNOSE to TP will ever return the same conflict set.
limits: Original pruning has a flaw (later corrected by Greiner, Smith and Wilkerson 1989; correction paper not opened this session). Breadth-first means diagnoses arrive in order of cardinality, which can stop at level k.
agent_relevance: Lazy conflict generation: do not enumerate all failure explanations; ask the checker for one conflict avoiding the current suspects, expand, repeat. Cheap and budgetable, with a depth cap k.

source: Reiter (1987) Section 5 Measurements (Theorems 5.7, Corollaries 5.8-5.9)
finding: A new measurement removes the diagnoses that predicted something else, keeps those that predicted it, but can ADD new diagnoses that are strict supersets of old rejected ones. So a naive divide-and-conquer on all diagnoses fails. For single-fault diagnoses it works exactly.
numbers: Davis device: measure out(M2)=5. All 4 old diagnoses predict not-5, and 4 new ones appear: {M1,M2,M3}, {M1,M2,A2}, {M2,M3,A1}, {M2,A1,A2}. Ex 5.10: {M1} predicts out(M1)=4, {A1} predicts 6; measuring 6 leaves {A1}, {M2,M3}, {M2,A2}.
quote: any new diagnosis resulting from the new measurement will be a strict superset of some old diagnosis
limits: Result is for weak-fault (normal-behaviour-only) models. The paper itself leaves open how to reuse the old HS-tree.
agent_relevance: Probing: a probe that kills every current suspect does not mean a bug-free answer. It raises the number of simultaneous faults. The agent should widen suspect size when all singletons die, not conclude 'impossible'.

source: Reiter (1987) Section 6 diagnosis and default logic (Theorem 6.1)
finding: Diagnosis is nonmonotonic: a new observation can leave none of the current diagnoses standing. Theorem 6.1: there is a 1-to-1 match between diagnoses and extensions of the default theory with defaults :not-AB(c)/not-AB(c), and extensions are exactly the sentences the diagnosis predicts. Theory works for any logic with binary semantics, and/or/not.
numbers: Theorem 6.1 proved by maximal-consistent-default argument.
quote: diagnostic reasoning is nonmonotonic
limits: Assumes a decidable consistency check for the chosen logic.
agent_relevance: Beliefs held as 'all steps normal unless shown otherwise' are defaults. Revising on a failed check is expected, not a failure. Supports a design where assumptions are retractable and tracked.

source: Reiter (1987) Section 7 related work: Davis, Genesereth, de Kleer, de Kleer and Williams, Poole, Ginsberg
finding: Reiter credits de Kleer (1976 LOCAL, SOPHIE) with the idea of conflict sets and Genesereth (DART) with first-order logic diagnosis and test generation. Davis's candidate generation (intersect conflicts, then suspend each candidate and test) is justified by Reiter's Theorem 4.12. De Kleer and Williams (GDE) independently reached Theorem 4.4 but, Reiter says, without formalization, and go beyond with probabilities of diagnoses and choice of next measurement. Davis handles single faults and bridge faults, which Reiter's fixed component list cannot.
numbers: Genesereth/Reiter differences listed: 4 (any logic, multiple faults, algorithm, measurement results).
quote: Our theory primarily builds upon, and generalizes, the work of de Kleer [5] and Genesereth [7].
limits: This is Reiter's own account of priority, not a neutral history. GDE and Davis papers not opened directly.
agent_relevance: Lineage for our notes: conflict (de Kleer 1976) then hitting set (Reiter 1987) then probability-guided probing (de Kleer and Williams 1987). The probing step is the one our schema lacks.

source: Grastien, Haslum, Thiebaux (2023, arXiv) A More General Theory of Diagnosis from First Principles
finding: Generalizes Reiter. Diagnosis = hypotheses supported by at least one behaviour consistent with the observation. Minimal diagnosis = most preferred candidates. If the hypothesis space is well partially ordered, the minimal diagnosis exists and is finite (Theorem 1). Search needs only a test oracle: does the diagnosis intersect this set of hypotheses? Failed tests return a conflict, a set of hypotheses proven to contain no candidate.
numbers: Theorems 1-10; strategies PLS, PLS+r, PFS, PFS+e, PFS+ec (preferred-first search with conflicts).
quote: the minimal diagnosis as the set of preferred diagnosis candidates in a search space of hypotheses
limits: Written for discrete event systems. Needs a sound test solver (SAT or heuristic search).
agent_relevance: The test-oracle view fits an agent: the oracle is a code checker. We only need 'does any answer in this family pass the checks?', and on failure a reason that rules out a whole family.

source: Grastien et al. (2023) experiments on power-network alarms (129 instances) and labour-market database cleansing (600 problems)
finding: Conflict-guided preferred-first search with a SAT test solver beat special-purpose algorithms. Junction tree solved only 23 of 129 power instances. Heuristic-search test solver is good at finding a candidate but no better than blind search at proving none exists. In the database task the largest minimal diagnosis had 12 faults and one instance had 450 minimal candidates.
numbers: 129 power instances, 2 to 146 alarms each, 2 to 104 relevant components; PFS+ec/SAT solved 12 more than BDD and 4 more than PFS with heuristic solver; PLS/H.S. had the full minimal diagnosis in 17% of unsolved-but-known cases, failing only on the last proof. 600 database problems, up to 6 automata of at most 6 states.
quote: heuristically guided state space search can be quite effective at finding a solution when one exists
limits: Not LLM work. Time limit 1800 s in the figure. Hardness depends on hypothesis space: sets easier than multisets easier than sequences.
agent_relevance: Finding a good candidate is cheap; proving none is better is the costly part. Agent should stop with a labelled best candidate, not claim minimality. 450 candidates shows we need a preference order to cut the list.

source: Grastien et al. (2023) Section 7.2 on de Kleer and Williams (1987), kernel diagnoses, ATMS
finding: Reiter's theory covers weak-fault models (only correct behaviour modelled). De Kleer and Williams extended to strong-fault models (fault behaviours modelled) using an ATMS that pre-computes all maximal conflicts. With weak faults, a superset of a candidate is a candidate (monotone), so minimal candidates summarise all. With strong faults this fails, so de Kleer, Mackworth, Reiter (1990/1992) introduced kernel diagnoses.
numbers: Example: over a multiset space with odd number of f2 faults, kernel diagnoses are infinite; maximal conflicts also infinite.
quote: Weak-fault models have a certain monotonicity property
limits: Secondary description by another group. Original GDE and DMR papers were not accessible in open text this session.
agent_relevance: If our scaffold models only 'what a correct step does', minimal suspects suffice. If it also models how steps typically go wrong (known failure modes), monotonicity breaks and we must not drop supersets.

source: Grastien et al. (2023) Section 7.3 related search algorithms: Bylander et al. 1991, SAFARI (Feldman et al. 2010)
finding: SAFARI and Bylander's method avoid the memory cost of all conflicts by finding any candidate and then walking to a smaller candidate among its parents. Guaranteed to return a minimal candidate under weak-fault models, but not all minimal candidates. SAFARI stops refinement once two parent checks fail.
numbers: Stop rule: two failed parent checks.
quote: This approach does not guarantee that all minimal candidates will be found.
limits: Stochastic and incomplete by design.
agent_relevance: A practical cheap loop for the agent: take any failing answer, greedily drop suspect steps while the checks still fail to pass, stop after two misses. Gives one minimal culprit set fast.

source: Sztyber-Betley et al. (2025) Are Diagnostic Concepts Within the Reach of LLMs? DX 2025, OASIcs 2:1-2:20
finding: Asks whether LLMs can produce MBD objects: incidence matrices, Minimal Structurally Overdetermined (MSO) sets, minimal conflicts and minimal diagnoses, graded against the Fault Diagnosis Toolbox and a hitting-set program. Defines R-conflict (Reiter's conflict) as the component support of an FMSO set whose test fails, and minimal diagnosis as a minimal hitting set of minimal R-conflicts.
numbers: 23 arithmetic and logic circuits; models 4o-mini (with code interpreter, temperature 0), o1 (run once, about 30 USD per iteration), o3-mini (10 runs each). Earlier gpt-4o and 4o-mini without code interpreter had near-zero accuracy on unseen examples.
quote: LLMs do not provide an alternative to diagnosis algorithms.
limits: Each step graded with correct inputs, so errors do not compound. Exploratory. Circuits are small; test cases hand-made after the models' release.
agent_relevance: Direct test of our split: model fills a slot, code does the algorithm. Even reasoning models are not reliable at the full pipeline, so hitting-set and consistency should be code.

source: Sztyber-Betley et al. (2025) results by task
finding: Incidence matrix generation: o1 and o3-mini reached perfect accuracy; 4o-mini added extra variables. MSO generation: o1 and o3-mini degrade as the number of relations grows. Conflict generation: o1 best, with an apparent rise with complexity that is an artifact of poor scores when there are zero conflicts. Diagnosis generation (hitting sets): clear drop with complexity; o3-mini best. Dedicated (circuit-specific) and broad prompts performed similarly.
numbers: Scores are F1 from precision and recall against ground truth. Exact per-model means appear only in figures (not extracted). Quality varies highly between runs.
quote: the quality of the results vary highly in different runs
limits: Numeric values are in plots only; I did not extract them. Cost and latency unbounded via API.
agent_relevance: Decoding the empty-conflict case matters: a model asked for a conflict when none exists invents one. Code must decide whether a conflict exists (the check), not the model.

source: Plank and Wotawa (2026) Using SLMs and LLMs for Diagnosis. DX 2026, OASIcs 14
finding: Text-only circuit diagnosis with 13 models (3 API LLMs, 10 small local models). Manual scoring 0-2 on correctness, completeness, reasoning, hallucination, uncertainty, clarity, weighted into W (correctness 30%, reasoning 20%, hallucination 20%, completeness 15%, uncertainty 10%, clarity 5%). Three tiers; larger models better. The prompt did not ask for subset-minimal answers, but scoring used the subset-minimal candidate set.
numbers: 7 systems, 2 scenarios mostly, 3 runs each, temperature 0.2, max 800 tokens. Gemini 2.5 Flash W=1.846 hit rate 79.5% hallucination rate 20.5%; Mistral Large W=1.832 hit 76.9% hallucination 15.4%; Llama 4 Scout 17B W=1.526 hit 38.5% hall 7.7%; Mistral 7B W=1.235 hit 25.6% hall 61.5%; TinyLlama 1.1B W=0.314 hit 0%; Llama 3.2 1B hallucination 94.9%.
quote: language models with more parameters achieve superior performance
limits: Manual scoring, one scorer apparently, small scenario set (39 scenario-runs per hit rate). Models in the circuit with 5 bulbs and 4 switches: all SLMs below 0.60.
agent_relevance: On tiny circuits big models do well, but hallucination is the cleanest quality signal. Evidence for enforcing G2: each named candidate must cite a given component or reading.

source: Plank and Wotawa (2026) failure to list multiple faults
finding: In Circuit 1 scenario 2 (both bulbs dark), only Gemini 2.5 Flash named the valid but unlikely double fault 'L1 and L2 both broken'. All other models gave only the most probable single candidates. Mistral 7B, the largest local model and 4th overall, dropped behind smaller ones on the 5-bulb circuit.
numbers: 1 of 13 models named the double fault in that scenario. Circuit 3: three API models above 1.70; all SLMs below 0.60. Rank-sum: Gemini 8, Mistral Large 15, Llama 4 Scout 26, TinyLlama 86.
quote: no model other than Gemini 2.5 Flash identified the theoretically valid, though unlikely, possibility
limits: Single scenario; judged manually against a hand-written expected set.
agent_relevance: Models favour likely single faults. Reiter's parsimony says singles first but multiple-fault diagnoses must stay reachable (Theorem 5.7). Code should force the size-2 level when singles are all refuted.

source: Dave, Nguyen, Vilim (2024) Integrating LLMs for Explainable Fault Diagnosis in Complex Systems. arXiv 2402.06695
finding: Pairs an existing consistency-based diagnoser (PRO-AID, physics-based, residuals from analytical redundancy relations) with an LLM agent and a symbolic engine. The LLM only explains diagnoses and answers operator questions; it queries the symbolic engine for facts to limit hallucination. Demonstrated on a faulty sensor in a molten sodium facility.
numbers: No accuracy figures in the sections read; a case demonstration only.
quote: we address the hallucination issues by constraining the output of the LLM
limits: Demonstration, not a benchmark. Context limit motivates giving the LLM only the needed slice (about 12 pages of text in context cited).
agent_relevance: Architecture match: diagnoser is code, LLM explains and queries. Supports 'model fills slot, program decides'.

source: Muehlburger and Wotawa (2024) FLEX: Fault Localization and Explanation Using Open-Source LLMs in Powertrain Systems
finding: Open-source LLMs with retrieval first infer rules from normal behaviour, then apply them to flag anomalies in battery and powertrain data. The first prompt worked on battery data but needed rewording for powertrain data; the rule-inference prompt improved powertrain detection.
numbers: Mistral 7B F1 up to 0.99; Llama3.1 8B-instruct-fp16 and Gemma 2 reached F1 1.0 in complex scenarios (abstract).
quote: significantly improved anomaly detection for the powertrain dataset
limits: Abstract-level numbers only read; detection (is something wrong) rather than isolation of the culprit.
agent_relevance: Learning 'normal behaviour' rules before checking is the weak-fault model step. Sensitive to prompt wording across domains.

source: Jha et al. (2025) ITBench: Evaluating AI Agents across Diverse Real-World IT Automation Tasks. arXiv 2502.05352
finding: Benchmark of 94 real-world IT scenarios. Fault diagnosis there means finding entities in a fault propagation chain. State-of-the-art agents solve few.
numbers: 42 SRE, 50 CISO, 2 FinOps scenarios; resolve rates 13.8% SRE, 25.2% CISO, 0% FinOps.
quote: resolve only 13.8% of SRE scenarios, 25.2% of CISO scenarios, and 0% of FinOps scenarios
limits: Agent resolve rate mixes diagnosis with mitigation. Models are those tested in early 2025.
agent_relevance: Shows how far ad-hoc LLM diagnosis agents are from solved on real systems, as a baseline for any scaffold claim.

source: Kim et al. (2026) Why Do AI Agents Systematically Fail at Cloud Root Cause Analysis? (OpenRCA process-level failure analysis)
finding: Ran the full OpenRCA benchmark on five LLMs and classified failures into 12 pitfall types in three groups (inside one agent, between agents, agent-environment). Top pitfalls, hallucinated data interpretation and incomplete exploration, persist for every model tier. Prompt engineering alone did not fix the dominant ones; a richer inter-agent communication protocol cut communication failures by up to 15 percentage points.
numbers: 1,675 agent runs; perfect-accuracy range 3.9% to 12.5% across five models.
quote: hallucinated data interpretation and incomplete exploration, persist across all models regardless of capability tier
limits: Failure labels were produced by the authors' analysis; mitigations tested on subsets.
agent_relevance: Failures come from the loop, not the model. Fixing it with program-controlled structure (what to look at next) beats prompt tweaks, in line with G1-G2.

source: Jha et al. (2026) Think Locally, Explain Globally: Graph-Guided LLM Investigations (EoG, Explanations over Graphs)
finding: ReAct agents are order-sensitive and non-deterministic on diagnosis over dependency graphs. EoG puts the LLM on local labelling (cause or symptom) and a deterministic controller on traversal, state and belief propagation, computing a minimal explanatory frontier. Frames investigation as abductive reasoning with non-monotonic belief revision.
numbers: Reliability gap (Pass@k minus Majority@k) of 14 points for Gemini 3 Flash up to 32 points for Gemini 2.5 Pro; best model Gemini 3 Flash 89% Pass@k but only 51% of scenarios consistently correct; EoG gives about 7x average gain in Majority@k F1 on ITBench diagnostics.
quote: separation of deterministic control flow (tool orchestration, state management) from non-deterministic reasoning (causal inference)
limits: Preprint. Numbers from figures and abstract; benchmark is ITBench subset.
agent_relevance: Closest LLM analogue of our design and of a Reiter-style minimal frontier. Evidence that code-controlled traversal fixes the Pass@k versus Majority@k gap.

source: Kim et al. (2025) TN-AutoRCA: Benchmark Construction and Agentic Framework for Alarm-Based RCA in Telecommunication Networks. arXiv 2507.18190
finding: 530 fault scenarios built from expert-validated knowledge graphs. Direct LLM prompting tops out below 70% F1. An agent that loops evaluate, analyze, repair on a code solution using contrastive feedback across all failures lifts F1.
numbers: Gemini-2.5-Pro direct: F1 58.99%; with Auto-RCA loop: F1 91.79%. Best direct models below 70% F1.
quote: elevating the final solution's F1-score on TN-RCA530 from a baseline of 58.99% ... to 91.79%
limits: Solution is code tuned on the same benchmark's failures, so generalisation beyond the 530 scenarios is not shown in the abstract.
agent_relevance: Fixing the checkable procedure from failing cases, not asking for a better single answer, is strong. Beware G3: tuning to the same cases can fit them.

source: Kang, Chen, Yoo, Lou (2023) Explainable Automated Debugging via LLM-driven Scientific Debugging (AutoSD). arXiv 2304.02195
finding: LLM proposes a hypothesis, runs the debugger to test it, observes, and concludes before patching. Ablating code execution makes runs less reliably plausible. A human study of 20 participants (6 professional developers) found no statistically significant gain from explanations for judging patches.
numbers: 73% of individual AutoSD runs gave a plausible patch; 63% when the debugger was ablated. 10 patch candidates beat Codex with 200 on Defects4J. Human study 20 participants, 12 bugs in two groups of six; 1045 plausible patches, 100 sampled by hand.
quote: incorporating code execution contributes to the reliability of AutoSD
limits: No significant benefit of explanations in the human study. Benchmarks are Defects4J, ARHE, BugsInPy.
agent_relevance: Diagnosis by hypothesise, test with real execution, conclude: a Reiter-style loop. Real output feedback raises plausible rate by 10 points (G2).

source: Gao et al. (2026) One Hypothesis Is Not Enough: Abductive Reasoning with Agentic Hypothesis Refinement over Knowledge Graphs (HypoAgent). arXiv 2605.31370
finding: Argues LLMs generate a well-formed hypothesis that may still fail to explain observations and have no mechanism to detect it. HypoAgent proposes, finds root cause by fragment-level coverage, and refines. Beats one-shot on BioKG, PharmKG8k and DBpedia50 in single-turn and multi-turn settings.
numbers: Gains stated qualitatively in the text I read; no figures extracted.
quote: A generated hypothesis may be well-formed and satisfy the given conditions yet still fail to explain the observations
limits: Abductive (explain the observation) rather than consistency-based. Knowledge-graph logic hypotheses.
agent_relevance: Supports G3 and checking coverage of the observation, which is the abductive complement of Reiter's consistency test.

source: Reiter (1987) Example 4.9 and Section 4.4: Davis multiplier-adder device
finding: Worked benchmark used by Davis, de Kleer and Williams, and Reiter. Three multipliers and two adders; inputs 3,2,3,2,3,2 give outputs 10 and 12 instead of 12 and 12. Four minimal diagnoses. Single-fault diagnoses are preferred because components fail independently. Predictions per diagnosis let a probe separate them.
numbers: 5 components. Observation out(A1)=10, out(A2)=12. {M1} predicts out(M2)=6 and out(M3)=4; {M2,M3} predicts out(M2)=4 and out(M3)=8. Two different pruned trees (Fig 9 and Fig 10) give the same 4 diagnoses.
quote: single fault diagnoses are judged more likely to be correct than any of their companion multiple fault diagnoses
limits: Independence of failures is an assumption; common-cause faults break it.
agent_relevance: Our model errors are not independent (G4). So 'fewest faults first' is only a heuristic for the agent, weaker than for hardware.

source: Reiter (1987) Section 2.4 and Section 6.1 on decidability and generality
finding: No decision procedure exists for first-order consistency, so general diagnosis is not computable. Practical settings are decidable: Boolean equations for switching circuits, linear equations for linear circuits. Theory also frames database integrity violations as a diagnosis problem, and time-varying devices with temporal logic.
numbers: Not applicable (theory).
quote: we should not allow the undecidability of the general problem to prevent us from developing a theory
limits: Each application needs its own decidability argument; heuristics when undecidable.
agent_relevance: The agent's checks must be decidable by code (run, compare, count). Where no checker exists the whole scheme degrades to model opinion, which G2 forbids.

source: Grastien et al. (2023) Section 3 Definition 1 vs abductive diagnosis and preference relations
finding: Consistency-based diagnosis is weaker than abductive diagnosis (Brusoni et al. 1998), which needs each candidate to imply part of the observation. Minimality uses a partial order of preference over hypotheses. Their suggested fix for 450 minimal candidates is to enrich the preference, for example prefer a hypothesis over another that has two more faults.
numbers: Max 450 minimal candidates and 12 faults per candidate in the labour-market data.
quote: this definition of diagnosis is weaker than that of an abductive diagnosis
limits: Consistency alone admits many unhelpful candidates, such as the empty fault claim that explains nothing.
agent_relevance: Use both: consistency (checks pass) and coverage (explains the failing observation). Add a preference order to rank the survivors.

source: Reiter (1987) Section 4.3 remark on caching and special-purpose provers
finding: The prover is a plug-in: any function TP that returns a conflict set or V. Constraint propagation (Davis, de Kleer and Williams) or Boolean solvers can serve. Results of earlier calls should be cached. If TP returns only minimal conflicts, no edge is ever marked redundant. The procedure can stop at level k to bound the fault size.
numbers: Remarks (1)-(4) in Section 4.3.
quote: The role of the theorem prover is simply to return a suitable conflict set when so requested
limits: Correctness proofs assume a sound and complete TP.
agent_relevance: Clean interface for the scaffold: checker returns a conflict or pass. The loop is generic, the checker is task-specific code.

source: Sztyber-Betley et al. (2025) related work on LLM fault diagnosis cited in the paper
finding: Authors state that earlier LLM fault-diagnosis works (explanations for nuclear plants, AutoFL, LLMAO, FD-LLM, FaultExplainer, FLEX, FaultLines, AAD-LLM) do not link LLM results to model-based diagnosis concepts. FaultExplainer reported hallucinations and reliance on PCA-selected features. Results in this field were closely tied to prompt design and text encoding.
numbers: No pooled numbers.
quote: none of these works really links LLM results to concepts developed in the field of model-based diagnostics
limits: Authors' own framing of a gap; a small literature in 2025.
agent_relevance: Our link between hitting-set diagnosis and LLM agents is largely unexplored: little prior art to copy, and no standard benchmark.
